clue.text: Angry Lancashire playwright's thoughtful gift to Pooh?

definitions.meaning: Shelagh Delaney of Salford, Lancashire, wrote this 1958 kitchen-sink play in the era of the Angry Young Men
Winnie-the-Pooh is greedy for the sweet stuff bees make, so a small sample of it would be a considerate present

explanation.surface: A cross northern dramatist is choosing a considerate present for a famous bear.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancashire then took in Salford, Delaney's home town; 'Angry' points to the Angry Young Men of late-1950s British drama.
explanation.definitionFit: One title names the Delaney play; the same words describe a little of the honeypot treat Pooh craves.

clue.text: One of those at Ludlow Fair who would never be old?

definitions.text: One of those at Ludlow Fair who would never be old?

parts.words: One of those at Ludlow Fair who would never be old?
parts.note: Housman's poem 'The lads in their hundreds to Ludlow come in for the fair' ends on the young men who will never grow old; one of them is a youth of that English county

explanation.surface: A question about a fairgoer in a market town who stayed forever young.
explanation.walkthrough: Ludlow is a market town in Shropshire, a county on the Welsh border; Housman's 1896 collection takes its title from such a young countryman.
explanation.definitionFit: Housman's poems picture young men of that border county, killed before they could grow old, as in the Ludlow fair poem.

clue.text: Roman courts used for Seneca trial

indicators.note: the letters are found already in place within the words that follow, used to supply the answer

explanation.surface: Ancient courts employed for the prosecution of the philosopher Seneca.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used for' tells you the letters are lying inside 'Seneca trial', across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: In a Roman house the central open courtyard was called by this Latin plural.

clue.text: Strong people in displacement

definitions.meaning: L. A. G. Strong wrote the novel 'The ...' (1945), so the name stands for his book
people who are moving from place to place, journeying

explanation.surface: Powerful individuals caught up in an enforced move of population.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strong' looks like an adjective but is the novelist L. A. G. Strong, whose 1945 novel won the James Tait Black Prize.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strong novel has this title, and people on the move are journeyers by definition.

clue.text: A Month in Languedoc to be remembered

indicators.note: in tells you the answer sits within the following words, running across their breaks

explanation.surface: A month spent in the south of France that will stay in the memory.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the end of 'Languedoc' and finishes on the first letter of 'remembered'. Languedoc is a region of southern France.
explanation.definitionFit: The tenth calendar period of the year is one of the twelve.

clue.text: A novel sort of rogue

parts.note: Hugh Walpole's 1930 novel 'Rogue ...' gives its rogue this surname, so he is a rogue found in a novel

explanation.surface: A new kind of scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' reads as 'new' but means a work of fiction: the rogue is the title character of Walpole's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis, the hero of Walpole's Lakeland saga, carries this family name and the nickname of a rogue.

clue.text: "What if 'is —' boyfriends spots us before?" (Margery Allingham, Sweet Danger)

definitions.text: "What if 'is —' boyfriends spots us before?" (Margery Allingham, Sweet Danger)

parts.words: "What if 'is —' boyfriends spots us before?" (Margery Allingham, Sweet Danger)
parts.note: the gap completes the jocular phrase 'his —', a mock title for a self-important man, dropped H and all

explanation.surface: A line of Cockney dialogue quoted from an Allingham thriller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His nibs' is a British slang mock title for a self-important man; the speaker drops the H.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation needs the word from the slang phrase used for a man who gives himself airs.

clue.text: Youthful notion of Frank Swinnerton

definitions.meaning: a concept or thought belonging to youth

explanation.surface: A juvenile thought put forward by the novelist Swinnerton.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase also comes from Thomson's line about teaching 'the young idea how to shoot', meaning young minds.
explanation.definitionFit: A youthful notion is literally a young thought, and Swinnerton used the phrase as a book title.

clue.text: Orchestra commemorated by Vaughan Williams and Haydn?

definitions.text: Orchestra commemorated by Vaughan Williams and Haydn?

parts.words: Orchestra commemorated by Vaughan Williams and Haydn?
parts.note: the capital city's famous orchestra shares its name with a symphony by each composer, as if both had written in its honour

explanation.surface: A question about a band celebrated by two great composers.
explanation.walkthrough: Vaughan Williams wrote 'A London Symphony' and Haydn's No 104 carries the city's name; drop the last word of the LSO's name and you have both.
explanation.definitionFit: Both composers wrote an orchestral work named after the British capital, which is also the orchestra's name less its last word.

clue.text: What love is not, according to Feste

definitions.text: What love is not, according to Feste

parts.words: What love is not, according to Feste
parts.note: Feste the clown sings in Twelfth Night 'What is love? 'Tis not —; Present mirth hath present laughter'

explanation.surface: A question about what Shakespeare's jester denied love to be.
explanation.walkthrough: Feste is the clown in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night; his song says love belongs to the present, not the future.
explanation.definitionFit: The song sets love in the present moment, unlike the time to come, the life after this one.

clue.text: Murdoch's heavyweight dreamer?

parts.note: Iris Murdoch wrote '... Dream', and the British heavyweight boxer Frank shared the forename

explanation.surface: A question about a big boxer with a head full of dreams, linked to Murdoch.
explanation.walkthrough: Iris Murdoch's 1969 novel is 'Bruno's Dream'; Frank Bruno was a British heavyweight boxing champion.
explanation.definitionFit: The dreamer of the Murdoch title and the boxer share one first name.

clue.text: Make speech in part of actor at Elsinore

indicators.note: part of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A player at Hamlet's castle has his share of the lines to deliver.
explanation.walkthrough: Elsinore is Hamlet's castle; the run starts inside 'actor' and finishes in 'at'.
explanation.definitionFit: To declaim or hold forth formally is to deliver an address.

clue.text: Writer revised with spirit

indicators.note: revised means changed, so the pen's letters are reworked into another order

parts.note: a Biro is a ballpoint pen, a thing that writes

explanation.surface: An author rewrote the piece with energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer' suggests an author but is a pen, the Biro, whose letters 'revised' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Dash and vigour are the sense of the musical word for liveliness.

clue.text: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats

definitions.text: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats

parts.words: Such a man is a paltry thing, said Yeats
parts.note: Yeats opens a stanza of 'Sailing to Byzantium' with 'An — man is but a paltry thing'

explanation.surface: A quotation from Yeats about a worthless sort of man.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from 'Sailing to Byzantium': 'An aged man is but a paltry thing, / A tattered coat upon a stick'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's paltry man is an old one, so the missing word means elderly.

clue.text: Intricate string-pulling by Vonnegut

definitions.meaning: a children's game making complicated figures by looping string between the fingers
Kurt Vonnegut's 1963 novel bears the name of the string game

explanation.surface: Elaborate behind-the-scenes manipulation carried out by an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'string-pulling' suggests using influence, but here it is literal: the game of looping string around the fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: The children's game makes elaborate figures from looped twine, and Vonnegut used its name for a novel.

clue.text: A mold's was bohemian, as were those of Buchan

definitions.text: A mold's was bohemian, as were those of Buchan

parts.words: A mold's was bohemian, as were those of Buchan
parts.note: Matthew Arnold's poem is 'The ...-Gipsy', and John Buchan's first book of essays was '... Gipsies'

explanation.surface: A literary note on wandering learned men in Arnold and Buchan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bohemian' points to gipsy: Arnold's poem has a single wandering Oxford student, Buchan's essays several.
explanation.definitionFit: Both titles pair the gipsy with a learned student, the man of books.

clue.text: Director finds impediment over one of The Birds

indicators.note: in a down entry, over puts the first piece above the second

parts.note: a hitch is a snag or obstacle
a cock is a male bird

explanation.surface: A film-maker meets a snag with one of the creatures from his own famous film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Birds' is the title of the director's own 1963 film, which makes the surface fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred, the master of suspense, was a film-maker.

clue.text: Greenwood's supporting actor, further characterized as "groom only"

definitions.text: Greenwood's supporting actor, further characterized as "groom only"

parts.words: Greenwood's supporting actor, further characterized as "groom only"
parts.note: Walter Greenwood wrote the comedy ... Room Only': the answer plus the letters of 'groom only' rebuilds that title

explanation.surface: A note on a performer in Greenwood's work described as nothing but a bridegroom.
explanation.walkthrough: Add 'g room only' to the answer and you get Greenwood's title; the actor is a substitute who stands in for another.
explanation.definitionFit: A substitute performer is a supporting player who replaces the star.

clue.text: Housman, say, some well known painter needed

indicators.note: some means a portion of the words that follow, where the answer is found already in place

explanation.surface: Housman, it seems, needs a famous artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housman' is the poet, but read it as 'houseman', a junior hospital doctor; the answer lies across 'painter needed'.
explanation.definitionFit: A junior doctor living in at a hospital is a houseman in British use, an intern in American.

clue.text: We're-to, and I think the other fellow just blinked " (Dean Rusk)

definitions.text: We're-to, and I think the other fellow just blinked " (Dean Rusk)

parts.words: We're-to, and I think the other fellow just blinked " (Dean Rusk)
parts.note: Rusk's remark in the Cuban missile crisis was 'We're — to —', with the same word in both gaps

explanation.surface: Dean Rusk's famous comment on the Cuban missile crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: The page has lost a word around the hyphen: the quotation is 'We're eyeball to eyeball, and I think the other fellow just blinked'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rusk pictured the two powers in a close face-to-face stare-down, as if their eyes were touching.

clue.text: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer

definitions.text: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer

parts.words: Its ranks could scarce forbear to cheer
parts.note: Macaulay's 'Horatius' says 'even the ranks of —  / Could scarce forbear to cheer' at the hero's courage

explanation.surface: An enemy army so impressed it almost applauded.
explanation.walkthrough: From Macaulay's 'Lays of Ancient Rome': the Etruscan army facing Horatius on the bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Macaulay's admiring ranks are the Etruscan army, the forces of that Italian region.

clue.text: Midterm re-examination is somewhat cut down

indicators.note: a re-examination looks at things over again, so the letters of the word before are gone through and rearranged

explanation.surface: A second test halfway through term is a bit shortened.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-examination' rearranges the letters of 'Midterm'.
explanation.definitionFit: Clipped or pared slightly is lightly reduced.

clue.text: Returning sound of nymph

definitions.meaning: a sound that bounces back off a surface
the mountain nymph of Greek myth who pined for Narcissus until only her voice remained

explanation.surface: A sound coming back from a nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: A reverberation is a sound that comes back, and the Greek nymph wasted to a voice repeating others.

clue.text: Novelist of priestly tribe

definitions.meaning: Primo ..., the Italian writer of 'If This Is a Man' and novels
the Israelite tribe from which priests and Temple servants came

explanation.surface: A writer descended from the priestly line.
explanation.definitionFit: Primo the Italian author has the surname, and it names the Hebrew priestly tribe of Moses and Aaron.

clue.text: The Sum of Things describing return of harness-race horse

indicators.note: return means the horse's name is read back to front

parts.note: a pacer is a horse trained for harness racing

explanation.surface: A summing-up describes a trotting horse coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return of' turns the harness-racing horse around. 'The Sum of Things' is also the title of an Olivia Manning novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A summary is a sum of things said: a short run-through.

clue.text: Drink in honour of Godwin hero

indicators.note: in puts the drink inside the honour's letters

parts.note: CB, Companion of the Bath, is a British honour
ale is a drink

explanation.surface: A toast raised to the hero of a Godwin novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in honour of' reads as a toast, but 'in' is the container and 'honour' is CB. Godwin's 1794 novel is 'Caleb Williams'.
explanation.definitionFit: William Godwin's novel 'Things as They Are' is better known by its hero's full name, Caleb Williams.

clue.text: Bad omen for submarine skipper

indicators.note: bad means in a poor state, so the letters of the word that follows are disordered

explanation.surface: An ill portent for the commander of an undersea vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges the letters of 'omen'. Jules Verne's captain commands the Nautilus.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's captain in 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea' commands the underwater ship Nautilus.

clue.text: Be very fond of a French illustrator

parts.note: Gustave Doré was a French engraver who illustrated the Bible and Dante

explanation.surface: Showing great affection for a particular French artist.
explanation.definitionFit: To love dearly is to be very fond of something.

clue.text: William Boyd's protected species

parts.note: William Boyd wrote the 1998 novel '...', named after the animal with a protective bony shell

explanation.surface: A creature from a William Boyd novel under conservation protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'protected' sounds like conservation law but means the animal's armoured shell.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal wears bony plates as armour, and Boyd's novel bears its name.

clue.text: Shattered Dylan, below keg, nevertheless with full cognizance

indicators.note: shattered means smashed to pieces, so the words that follow are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A singer, exhausted and lying beneath a beer barrel, still knows exactly what he is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'below' looks like a position word but is part of the fodder: 'Shattered' rearranges DYLAN, BELOW and KEG together.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting with full awareness is acting in an informed, well-versed manner.
